sorular.konu: Inference-time control via prompting and prompt structure
sorular.soru: In which of the following situations is prompting (inference-time control) NOT sufficient on its own?
secenekler: When safety or style behavior must generalize across all inputs
When the output must be returned in a specific label format every time
When temporary context should be used only for that single request
When a small change in behavior needs to be tried out quickly
sorular.aciklama: Prompting suits fast iteration, task-specific formatting, small behavior changes, and temporary context, but it falls short for generalization of safety/style behavior, default reliability, or subjective preferences. A label-format constraint is exactly the 'task-specific formatting' area where prompting is strong.

sorular.soru: With the same prompt and model, raising the temperature makes sampled outputs more varied, yet greedy decoding still returns exactly the same token as before. Which mechanism explains both observations?
secenekler: Temperature removes low-probability tokens from the eligible set, so sampling varies while the top token is untouched
Temperature reorders the tokens at random, while greedy decoding ignores the new order and reads the original scores
Temperature changes how concentrated the probabilities are but keeps their ranking, so the top token stays the same
Temperature adjusts the model weights for that request only, which alters sampling but leaves greedy decoding fixed
sorular.aciklama: Temperature only makes the next-token distribution sharper or flatter: a flatter distribution gives lower-ranked tokens more chance under sampling, but the order of tokens is preserved, so greedy decoding keeps picking the same top token. Removing tokens from the eligible set is what top-k and top-p filtering do, not temperature.

sorular.soru: At one generation step the model is very confident in a single token; at another step the probability is spread over many tokens. Why does top-p filtering behave differently from top-k across these two steps?
secenekler: Top-p keeps a fixed number of tokens, whereas top-k keeps adding tokens until a probability threshold is reached
Top-p keeps the smallest set reaching a mass threshold, so its size follows the distribution; k is a fixed count
Top-p flattens the distribution before filtering, whereas top-k sharpens it, so the eligible sets end up different
Top-p always selects the single most likely token, whereas top-k samples uniformly among the k highest-ranked ones
sorular.aciklama: Top-p uses a probability threshold, so a peaked distribution needs only a few tokens to reach it while a flat one needs many; top-k keeps the same number of tokens regardless of the shape. The first option swaps the two definitions, and neither filter reshapes the distribution; they only restrict which tokens are eligible before renormalizing and sampling.

sorular.soru: Consider zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompts for a sentiment task with the instruction 'Return only the label' and the test input 'It was average.', containing 0, 1, and 3 examples respectively. What exactly is the difference among the three prompts?
secenekler: The instruction becomes slightly more detailed at each level; the number of examples is kept fixed
In one-shot a label list is given instead of an example; in few-shot, examples are added to it
In few-shot the examples are used as training data for a short-lived weight update of the model's parameters
The instruction and the new query stay fixed; only the number of input→output examples in the prompt changes
sorular.aciklama: In all three prompts the instruction ('Return only the label') and the test input ('It was average.') are identical; the only thing that changes is the 0, 1, or 3 examples added to the prompt. ICL performs no weight update (it is temporary task adaptation without a parameter update), so the option describing few-shot as training misrepresents the mechanism.

sorular.soru: Two few-shot prompts contain the same three demonstrations (Positive, Negative, Neutral); in the second, only the order is reversed. What does this pair test, and why is only the order changed?
secenekler: Majority-label bias; with the label distribution fixed, reordering isolates the effect of the majority label alone
Recency bias; with the label distribution held constant, any difference can be attributed only to the last demo
Recency bias; because reordering also changes the label distribution, both biases are measured at the same time
Majority-label bias; when the last example is Neutral, the model perceives the majority label as Neutral and favors it
sorular.aciklama: The C–D pair is a recency bias test: since the demos and label distribution stay the same, any change in prediction can be due to the most recently seen label, with no other variable involved. Majority-label bias is tested in the A–B pair by changing the label distribution; reordering the same demos does not change the label distribution, so the two biases are not measured together.

sorular.konu: Reasoning prompts: CoT, Self-Consistency, ToT, Least-to-Most, PAL
sorular.soru: Self-consistency samples several reasoning paths for one question and takes a majority vote over their final answers instead of trusting a single greedy path. What is the logic behind this design?
secenekler: The longest sampled path contains the most steps, so its final answer is treated as the most carefully checked one
Each path is scored at its intermediate steps, so weak branches are pruned before the remaining answers are counted
Different correct paths tend to reach the same answer while mistakes scatter, so agreement signals a reliable answer
Sampling makes each later path more concentrated, so the answer generated last is taken as the most reliable one
sorular.aciklama: Self-consistency marginalizes over the reasoning paths: how an answer was reached is ignored and only the final answers are counted, because many different valid routes converge on the correct answer while errors tend to disagree with each other. Scoring and pruning intermediate steps describes Tree of Thoughts, not self-consistency.

sorular.konu: Reasoning prompts: CoT, Self-Consistency, ToT, Least-to-Most, PAL
sorular.soru: Self-consistency also generates multiple reasoning paths. Which is the key mechanism that distinguishes Tree of Thoughts (Game of 24 example) from self-consistency?
secenekler: Generating paths independently from start to finish and voting over the final answers only at the end
Decomposing the question into subquestions and adding each answer to the prompt of the next subquestion
Writing the reasoning steps as program statements and leaving the final computation to an interpreter
Scoring intermediate steps with a value prompt and pruning unpromising branches without expanding them
sorular.aciklama: ToT generates candidate steps with a propose prompt and evaluates partial solutions as sure/likely/impossible with a value prompt (e.g., '10 13 13 → impossible'), expanding only the promising branches. Self-consistency has no intermediate-step evaluation; complete paths are generated independently and voted on at the end. Decomposing into subquestions describes Least-to-Most, and program statements describe PAL.

sorular.konu: Reasoning prompts: CoT, Self-Consistency, ToT, Least-to-Most, PAL
sorular.soru: A team observes that the model sets up the steps of word problems correctly but makes errors in the computation and in arithmetic that handles signs such as 'returned' (in a bakery example, CoT gives 62 while the correct answer is 74). Which reasoning-prompt approach directly addresses this problem?
secenekler: Increasing the number of chain-of-thought examples; seeing more rationales is expected to reduce arithmetic errors
Tree of Thoughts: scoring each arithmetic step as sure/likely/impossible and eliminating the faulty branch early
PAL: writing the steps as variable assignments and code, with the Python interpreter doing the final computation
pass@k: sampling k different solutions and selecting the answer that passes the unit tests as the final response
sorular.aciklama: PAL (Gao et al., 2023) converts natural-language reasoning into program statements (loaves_baked = 200, loaves_returned = 6, answer = ...); the computation is done by the interpreter rather than the model, and print(answer) gives 74. ToT is a search/pruning method and does not verify arithmetic; pass@k is an evaluation metric, not a prompting technique, and requires unit tests.

sorular.konu: Reasoning prompts: CoT, Self-Consistency, ToT, Least-to-Most, PAL
sorular.soru: In the two-stage structure of Least-to-Most prompting (Zhou et al., 2022), what is done in Stage 2?
secenekler: The subquestions are solved independently in parallel and the results are combined at the end
The subquestions are solved in sequence; each subquestion's answer is added to the next subquestion's prompt
Many solution paths are sampled and a majority vote is taken over the subquestion answers
Solving starts from the hardest subquestion; the main answer is obtained at the very start by working backward
sorular.aciklama: Stage 1 decomposes the question into subquestions; in Stage 2 the subquestions are solved in order from easy to hard, and the previous answer ('each trip takes 5 minutes') is added to the prompt to answer the next subquestion (15 ÷ 5 = 3). Parallel/independent solving breaks this chain; 'least-to-most' in the name means ordering from easy to hard, not hard to easy.

sorular.konu: Controlled evaluation in prompt engineering (DEV / TEST)
sorular.soru: Prompt B scores 84% accuracy on the DEV set and 79% on the held-out TEST set. What is the purpose of selecting the prompt on DEV, freezing it, and then evaluating it on TEST only once?
secenekler: To prevent the selection process on DEV from leaking into TEST, so the TEST score is an uninflated estimate of generalization
To prevent TEST from coming out lower than DEV; since both sets come from the same distribution, the scores are expected to be equal
To re-tune the decoding settings on TEST so that the 79% score moves closer to the 84% on DEV
To reuse the TEST set for every prompt version so as to obtain a more reliable average score
sorular.aciklama: Because the prompt was iteratively selected on DEV, the DEV score is optimistic (selection bias); if TEST is examined only once with the frozen prompt, 79% is a realistic estimate of generalization, and a DEV–TEST gap is expected. Reusing TEST for every version turns it into a second DEV; a controlled comparison also requires the model, decoding, examples, evaluator, and metric to be held fixed.

sorular.konu: Evaluation basics: task types, Accuracy, Exact Match, F1
sorular.soru: A model answers a numeric question with a full sentence that contains the right number. Exact Match gives the answer 0, while token-level F1 gives it partial credit. What explains the difference?
secenekler: Exact Match compares meanings through embeddings, whereas token F1 compares only the lengths of the two strings
Exact Match is averaged over several sampled outputs, whereas token F1 is decided by the first generated token
Exact Match rewards recall of the reference tokens, whereas token F1 rewards only precision of predicted tokens
Exact Match is all-or-nothing on the whole string, whereas token F1 credits each overlapping token separately
sorular.aciklama: Exact Match is 1 only when the prediction string equals the target, so a correct answer with different wording scores 0 unless a normalization step is defined beforehand; token F1 combines precision and recall over shared tokens, so the matching number still earns credit. Neither metric looks at meaning, and F1 uses both precision and recall, not precision alone.

sorular.konu: Reference-based metrics: BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, chrF, BERTScore
sorular.soru: BLEU is built on the n-gram precision of the candidate with respect to the reference. What would go wrong if its brevity penalty were removed?
secenekler: A very short candidate made of a few safe reference words could score highly while omitting most of the content
A very long candidate could repeat a reference word many times and be rewarded again for each single repetition
A paraphrased candidate built from synonyms would receive full credit although no surface n-grams overlap at all
A candidate with the right words in scrambled order would receive the same score at every n-gram order considered
sorular.aciklama: Precision only asks how many candidate n-grams appear in the reference and has no recall term, so dropping words never hurts it; the brevity penalty is what punishes candidates shorter than the reference. Rewarding repeated words is prevented by clipping the n-gram counts, which is a separate component from the brevity penalty.

sorular.konu: Reference-based metrics: BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, chrF, BERTScore
sorular.soru: For the same reference–candidate pair, ROUGE-1 Recall is 0.833, METEOR ≈ 0.820, and BLEU-1 is 0.819. Which property distinguishes METEOR from BLEU and is also its key limitation?
secenekler: It aligns stems and synonyms in word matching; therefore it depends on alignment resources and language
It uses character n-grams; therefore surface overlap does not guarantee semantic overlap in meaning
It relies on contextual token similarity; therefore high similarity does not imply correctness or entailment
It measures only n-gram/LCS coverage; therefore high overlap does not guarantee faithfulness to the source
sorular.aciklama: Besides exact matching, METEOR aligns stems and synonyms and weights recall more heavily (Fmean = 10PR/(R+9P)); these alignment resources make it language- and resource-dependent. Character n-grams define chrF, contextual token similarity defines BERTScore, and n-gram/LCS coverage defines ROUGE, along with their respective limitations.

sorular.soru: For a code benchmark, k programs are sampled for each task and pass@k is reported. Why is success counted per task instead of as the share of all generated programs that pass?
secenekler: Because the unit tests can be executed only once per task, the remaining sampled programs are never actually run
Because the k programs are merged into one final program, only a single combined result exists for every task
Because the metric asks whether a task gets solved within k tries, a single passing attempt settles that task
Because k is the number of unit tests per task, a task passes only when all k of those tests are satisfied
sorular.aciklama: pass@k measures success with up to k tries: a task succeeds when at least one of its k independently sampled solutions passes the unit tests, so failed attempts on a solved task do not count against it. k counts attempts, not tests, which is why the last option confuses the two, and the result is only as trustworthy as the tests themselves.

sorular.soru: A generated summary contains a statement that is true in the real world but appears nowhere in the retrieved passages. How does a groundedness check treat this statement, and why?
secenekler: As supported, because faithfulness is in the end a measure of whether the claims hold in the real world
As unsupported, because faithfulness measures consistency with the given evidence, not real-world truth
As false, because any claim that is missing from the provided source is taken as contradicted by it
As a safety violation, because adding outside content counts as obeying an injected instruction
sorular.aciklama: Groundedness asks whether each claim follows from the provided evidence, so a claim absent from the source is unsupported even if it happens to be true. The same logic works in the other direction: being unsupported by this source does not make a claim false, so labeling it as contradicted confuses support with truth.

sorular.soru: Two raters give the same Yes/No label to a large share of model answers. Why can this raw percent agreement overstate how reliable the annotation is, and what does Cohen's kappa correct?
secenekler: Percent agreement ignores how many items were rated; kappa rescales the agreement by the size of the sample
Percent agreement treats human labels as ground truth; kappa swaps them for labels produced by an LLM judge
Part of the agreement would occur by chance given how often each rater uses a label; kappa removes that part
Percent agreement counts only the Yes/Yes matches; kappa adds the No/No matches that the raw figure leaves out
sorular.aciklama: Raters who each use the labels at certain rates would agree on some items even if they labeled independently, and this expected chance agreement grows when both favor the same label; kappa reports only the agreement beyond chance, so it is 0 at chance level and can even be negative. Raw agreement already counts both Yes/Yes and No/No matches, so the last option misdescribes it.

sorular.konu: LLM-as-a-Judge: rubric, judge biases, and reporting
sorular.soru: A pairwise LLM judge prefers Answer A in the 1st position in Trial 1; in Trial 2, where the positions of A and B are swapped, it prefers Answer B in the 1st position. Which interpretation and check is correct?
secenekler: Verbosity bias; an explicit item penalizing irrelevant length should be added to the rubric to counter it
Self/style bias; since the judge picks the answer closer to its own style, judges from different models should be added
The judge is consistent; choosing the 1st position even after the order is swapped indicates a stable preference
Suspected position bias; the winner changes with the presentation order, so an A/B swap check should be applied
sorular.aciklama: A fair pairwise judge should prefer the same answer even when the order changes while the content stays the same; if the winner changes with position, position bias should be investigated and an A/B order-swap check should be applied. 'Always choosing the 1st position' is not consistency but precisely a symptom of position bias; the checks for verbosity and self/style bias address different problems.

sorular.konu: LLM-as-a-Judge: rubric, judge biases, and reporting
sorular.soru: A panel of LLM judges built from three different models prefers Answer A by a 2-to-1 majority. Why should validation on a human-labeled subset still be performed when reporting this result?
secenekler: Majority voting does not remove the judges' shared systematic errors; the panel must also be validated against humans
Since the panel lowers inference cost, the budget saved should be allocated to human evaluation
Since human labels are automatically treated as ground truth, the judge scores should be replaced directly with them
Since a 2/3 majority corresponds to κ = 0.60, it falls below the threshold; κ must be raised using human labels
sorular.aciklama: Diversity matters, but several judges can still share the same systematic errors, and validation on a human-labeled subset is the check against 'weak validation' of the judge; majority voting does not eliminate shared biases. The panel does not reduce cost but brings more inference cost; human labels are not automatically ground truth either; and relating a 2/3 majority to kappa confuses the concepts.
